reviewed the mentioned ticket https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1533

> "items for SQL injection, LDAP injection, SMTP injection,... but we don’t have an item for JNDI injection."

The comparison with other injections (sql, smtp…) is misleading. SQL, LDAP, SMTP are language(java, c#, python...) agnostic injections, but JNDI only works with JAVA for dynamic resolution or others which is a distinct vulnerability than traditional injection attacks. 
Rather than "JNDI injection," a more accurate term is "exploitation via insecure JNDI lookups" or something else I think.

If ASVS adds rules like 1.3.8 (JNDI) as a "special highlight" due to Log4Shell (I assume), should ASVS wait for a major exploit in other tech stacks before write rules for those resolution mechanisms?

If we wanted this requirement to more actionable, I would suggest something along the lines of:

_Verify that all input is sanitized, validated and/or escaped before being used in Java Naming and Directory Interface (JNDI) lookups, and ensure that JNDI is securely configured to disallow remote lookups and restrict access to trusted local resources only, to prevent JNDI injection attacks._

This is not the best version, but it highlights the direction we need to move in if we want this to be a more actionable requirement for developers.

Josh, I don’t think anything outside of JNDI/Log4Shell has been as catastrophic. That remote class-loading flaw was unique.But there are meaningful examples in other ecosystems that go beyond “just LDAP injection,” and they carry real security impact:

- .NET Active Directory lookups. Concatenated user input into LDAP filter queries (classic LDAP injection) is well known, but there are also service-binding abuses where untrusted input controls which directory object is resolved.
- Kubernetes DNS service discovery. Several CVEs (CVE-2019-11253 “Billion Laughs” in kube-api and related DNS resolution bugs) show that maliciously crafted names or records can force denial of service or redirection.
- Service registries (Consul, Eureka, Zookeeper). Attacks where an attacker injects/poisons service names, tricking consumers into connecting to hostile endpoints. Often called “service discovery poisoning,” the mechanism is the same pattern: untrusted input in a name/lookup API.
- Cloud directory/identity APIs (Azure AD Graph, AWS IAM Identity Center): Injection or manipulation of untrusted query parameters can yield data exfiltration or escalation. These are usually JSON/Graph query injections, but the “naming/directory lookup injection” framing fits.

This is why I lean toward one generic requirement with JNDI called out as the example. It avoids being Java-only, ties to existing LDAP injection requirements, and helps developers recognize that any lookup service can be a dangerous sink.
